facts.title: Velvet Revolver Audition and Trust (2003)
facts.body: Scott Weiland initially disliked the music sent by the future Velvet Revolver members but agreed to jam after hearing a second, improved CD. Despite arriving hours late due to drug use, he found the chemistry with Duff McKagan, Slash, Matt Sorum, and Dave Kushner to be "bang on" and trusted Matt Sorum from a shared rehab experience. "Besides, he'd been in rehab with Matt Sorom so he trusted him."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Scott Weiland

facts.title: Motivation to Join Velvet Revolver (2003)
facts.body: Scott Weiland was motivated to join Velvet Revolver not only by the promising musical chemistry and the fact that all other members were clean (offering a potentially supportive environment), but also by the "really good" money, given his previous extensive spending on drugs. "And besides, the money was really good. Really good. And Scott had no idea how many millions he'd already spent on drugs. Several."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Scott Weiland

facts.title: Duff McKagan's Intervention and Martial Arts Training (2003)
facts.body: After an initial rehab stint for Velvet Revolver's debut album didn't work, Duff McKagan took Scott Weiland to a rural retreat in Washington state. There, a martial arts expert's intense physical training regimen helped Weiland get "straight and healthy again," leading him to find his own trainer in LA. "Duff took him to a quiet rural place in Washington state to commune with his trainer, a martial arts expert who promised that Scott would work out his issues with him intense physical training."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Scott Weiland

facts.title: Arrest for Heroin Possession (Mid-2003)
facts.body: Approximately a month after Velvet Revolver's song "Let Me Free" was released for "The Hulk" soundtrack, Scott Weiland was arrested again for having heroin in his car. This resulted in probation, conditioned on his sobriety. "Let me free the first example of Velvet Revolver, which saw the light of day about a month after Scott was arrested again for having heroin in his car."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Scott Weiland

facts.title: Arrest for Hitting Parked Car (October 27, 2003)
facts.body: On October 27, 2003, after midnight in Hollywood, Scott Weiland hit a parked car and was arrested. He was sent to residential rehab to detox, with a judge allowing him four hours a day to leave the facility to finish recording Velvet Revolver's debut album. "While driving somewhere in Hollywood after midnight, Scott hit a parked car. He was arrested again and sent to what's called residential rehab to detox yet again."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Scott Weiland

facts.title: Kicking Heroin in Rehab (Late 2003)
facts.body: During his residential rehab stint in late 2003, which coincided with the final stages of recording Velvet Revolver's debut album, Scott Weiland reportedly kicked his heroin addiction. "However, stories from all corners do corroborate on one thing. That did kick heroin during this rehab stint."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Scott Weiland

facts.title: Relationship Improvement and Financial Woes with Mary (Late 2003)
facts.body: During this period, Scott Weiland's relationship with Mary Forsberg improved after being on the rocks. They sold their San Diego home to cover bills, including legal fees for a planned divorce that ultimately did not occur. "They sold their San Diego home to pay for a bunch of bills, including some lawyers for a divorce that they were going to get, but never happened."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Scott Weiland

facts.title: Post-Divorce Litigation (2003)
facts.body: After Chris Cornell and Susan Silver divorced in 2003, a lawsuit ensued. Chris sued for $1 million in damages, alleging that Silver, as Soundgarden's manager, diverted money owed to him to other band members. facts.title: Early Years and Major Label Signing (2003)
facts.body: The band toiled in obscurity for "eight, nine years" before their major label career began in the fall of 2003. Their break came when producer Gavin Brown and Mike McCarty saw them, leading to demo recordings and a publishing deal. Warner Canada then became interested due to their "first right of refusal" on the demos. The band experienced a "bidding war" involving Atlantic, Elektra, and Warner Brothers (US) over a month in August, with them being flown to New York for fancy dinners and performances. They were a "working class" band, all around 26 years old at the time, which made the experience surreal. "we went from toiling an obscurity for eight, nine years to then all of a sudden, literally within two weeks being flown back and forth to New York for a whole month, the whole month of August."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Billy Talent In Their Own Words: Part 2
facts.name: Billy Talent

facts.title: Evolution of Music Consumption (2003-2012)
facts.body: The band has witnessed significant technological shifts in the music industry since the birth of the internet, including the rise of iPhones, streaming services, Facebook, MySpace, and Twitter by 2012. They acknowledge that record sales have never been their primary source of income, instead relying heavily on touring since their inception in 2003.
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Comedy Central Promo Origin of Hate (2003)
facts.body: One theory for the widespread hatred attributes its origin to a Comedy Central promo for the show "Tough Crowd," featuring Colin Quinn, which began airing on May 5, 2003. In the promo, Quinn humorously linked violent music to violent behavior, quipping that "bad music makes bad music," and specifically, "listening to Nickelback makes me want to kill Nickelback." This coincided with Nickelback's explosion in popularity with their "Silver Side Up" album and hit single "How You Remind Me." "For the answer, we probably have to go back to Comedy Central, the American TV channel, back in 2003. The channel ran a promo for a show called Tough Crowd featuring Colin Quinn. In this promo, he referenced a study that linked violent music to violent behavior. I quote, no one talks about the studies that show that bad music makes bad music. But listening to Nickelback makes me want to kill Nickelback."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Formation as a Supergroup (2003)
facts.body: Formed in 2003, Velvet Revolver began with former Guns N' Roses members Duff McKagan, Slash, and Matt Sorum, who then recruited Dave Kushner from Wasted Youth. They auditioned several singers, including Josh Todd of Buckcherry, Travis Meeks of Days of the New, and B-Real of Cypress Hill, before settling on Scott Weiland. "Susan told Mary that three guys from Guns and Roses had kissed and made up and were forming a new band."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Velvet Revolver

facts.title: Scott Weiland's Initial Reluctance and Trust (2003)
facts.body: Scott Weiland initially disliked the music presented by the band, but a second demo convinced him to jam. He showed up late due to drug use, but found unexpected chemistry and a low ego factor, particularly trusting Matt Sorum due to a shared rehab experience. "Matt, to Scott's surprise, the ego factor was low and the chemistry was bang on. Besides, he'd been in rehab with Matt Sorom so he trusted him."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Velvet Revolver

facts.title: Band Members' Sobriety (2003)
facts.body: The members of Velvet Revolver (McKagan, Slash, Sorum, Kushner) were all 100% clean from drugs at the time of their formation, providing a potential environment to help Scott Weiland get clean as well. "And all the other guys had been in trouble with drugs too and were all 100% clean. So maybe this was the environment that would help him get clean too."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Velvet Revolver

facts.title: Scott Weiland's Rehab Before Debut Album (2003)
facts.body: Prior to recording their debut album, Scott Weiland underwent another trip to rehab to get straight. When that proved insufficient, Duff McKagan arranged for him to train with a martial arts expert in Washington state, which helped Weiland achieve sobriety and health. "First there was another trip to rehab to straighten out a bit before the band got to work on their debut album."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.name: Velvet Revolver

facts.title: Movie Soundtrack Debut (2003)

facts.title: iTunes Music Store and iPod Launch (2003)
facts.body: Apple, under Steve Jobs, emerged as the savior of the recorded music industry by introducing the iTunes music store in April 2003 (initially Mac-only, then Windows in October). This followed the earlier release of the iTunes media player and the iPod, which was marketed as holding "a thousand songs in your pocket." Jobs convinced the five major record labels in 2002 to license their music, selling songs for 99 cents with Apple taking 30%. This move changed everything, leading to the iPod becoming the fastest-selling consumer electronic product and providing the first effective solution to music piracy by offering legal, clean digital tracks. "the iTunes music store was introduced in April 2003."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.body: The famous cover art for Blur's album Think Tank was created directly by Banksy, not merely inspired by his style, for which he received a significant payment. "la famosa portada del Cintan la hizo Basky pero el Basky me verdad no está inspirado en Basky sino que es Basky quien hizo esta portada y ganó bastante dinero a cien gra."
facts.episode: Blur - Think Tank y su dificil grabación.
facts.name: Banksy

facts.title: Think Tank (2003) Cover and Back Cover Artwork Payment
facts.body: Banksy was paid a substantial amount for designing both the front and back covers of Blur's Think Tank, which subsequently became an iconic image in music history. "Le pagaron mucha dinero por hacer lo que fue la portada del Cintan y la contraportada del Cintan y la verdad es que la portaba y el diés un icono de la historia de la música."
